stories.bridge: Every expected value you will compute in this course descends from those letters. Now let's learn to think the way Pascal and Fermat had to invent — from nothing, about uncertainty itself.

figures.name: Christiaan Huygens
figures.role: Dutch physicist; wrote the first probability textbook

stories.hook: In the summer of 1654, two Frenchmen who had never met began trading letters about a dice game — and invented probability.
stories.narrative: The problem came from a gambler, the Chevalier de Méré, who asked Blaise Pascal a question about an interrupted game: if two players must stop before finishing, how should the stakes be fairly divided? Pascal — twenty-one, already famous for his work on vacuum and calculating machines — wrote to Pierre de Fermat, a lawyer in Toulouse who did mathematics as a hobby and happened to be one of the sharpest minds in Europe. Their correspondence, through the summer and autumn of 1654, did something no one had done before: it reasoned systematically about events that had not happened yet. To split the stakes fairly, they had to weigh possible futures — and in doing so they invented the concept of expected value, the idea that an uncertain outcome has a precise mathematical worth. Pascal's triangle, that familiar array of numbers, became in their hands a machine for counting futures. Neither man published the letters as a theory; that fell to the Dutchman Christiaan Huygens, who turned their ideas into the first probability textbook, 'De ratiociniis in ludo aleae,' in 1657. Half a century later, Jacob Bernoulli's 'Ars Conjectandi,' published posthumously in 1713, proved the law of large numbers — the guarantee that averages settle down as trials accumulate — and Pierre-Simon Laplace's great treatise of 1812 turned the whole subject into an engine for science, from astronomy to demography. The final polish came in 1933, when the Russian Andrey Kolmogorov wrote probability down as pure axioms: a sample space, events, a measure. Three lines, and three centuries of gambling, astronomy, and argument were formalized. But the human core never changed: two men, by mail, asking what a future that might not happen is worth. Every risk model, every machine-learning classifier, every A/B test you will ever run is their correspondence, industrialized.
stories.title: The story behind probability
verifiedClaims: Pascal and Fermat's correspondence on the problem of points took place in 1654
Huygens published the first probability textbook in 1657
Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi (1713) contains the law of large numbers

stories.bridge: That is the quant's deepest trick: when the equation won't yield, simulate the world and count. Keep Ulam's solitaire in mind — we're about to build the same machinery, deliberately.
stories.hook: In 1946, Stanislaw Ulam lay in a hospital bed recovering from brain surgery, playing solitaire — and found himself wondering about the odds.
stories.narrative: Ulam was one of the brilliant exiles at Los Alamos, the laboratory that had built the atomic bomb — a Polish mathematician who had fled Europe in the 1930s and talked his way into the Manhattan Project on the strength of sheer ability. Recovering from brain surgery in 1946, he passed the time with card games and began wondering about a simple question: what is the probability that a given solitaire layout can be played to completion? The combinatorics were hopeless — far too many possible orderings to enumerate by hand, a number with dozens of digits. Then came the sideways thought that changed computational science: instead of calculating the probability analytically, deal out thousands of random layouts and count how many succeed. The fraction that wins estimates the probability. It was statistics as a substitute for combinatorics. He mentioned the idea to John von Neumann, who immediately saw something bigger. The newborn electronic computers — ENIAC and its successors — were perfect for exactly this: grinding through random trials at inhuman speed. The first serious application was neutron diffusion in nuclear weapons work, a problem as intractable as the solitaire game: neutrons scattering through matter in ways no equation could track. They needed a code name, and Ulam — whose uncle was a gambler — suggested 'Monte Carlo,' after the casino. The method worked so well it became one of the pillars of scientific computing, and von Neumann and Ulam's 1949 paper made it official. Today Monte Carlo simulation prices derivatives on Wall Street, models climate, renders the lighting in films, and plans radiation therapy. All of it descends from a convalescent mathematician, a deck of cards, and the realization that randomness, sampled patiently enough, becomes knowledge. The method's first published form came in 1949, when Metropolis and Ulam formalized it — and Nicholas Metropolis would soon give the world the Metropolis algorithm, Monte Carlo's most famous child. Keep the lineage straight when you use it in quant work: simulation doesn't replace mathematics, it replaces the mathematics you cannot do.
stories.title: The story behind the Monte Carlo method
verifiedClaims: Ulam conceived the method in 1946 while recovering from brain surgery
It was developed with von Neumann at Los Alamos, first applied to neutron diffusion
The name honors the Monte Carlo casino, suggested for Ulam's gambler uncle

stories.bridge: Zero looks like nothing, but it is the most powerful symbol in your toolkit. Now let's put it to work — trade math runs on place value, and place value runs on this.

figures.name: Brahmagupta
figures.role: Indian astronomer-mathematician; first to treat zero as a number

figures.name: al-Khwarizmi
figures.role: Persian scholar; transmitted Indian numerals through Arabic mathematics

stories.hook: In the year 628, an Indian astronomer wrote down the rules for arithmetic with nothing.
stories.narrative: Brahmagupta directed an astronomical observatory in Ujjain, in what is now central India, and in 628 he completed the Brahmasphutasiddhanta — 'the corrected treatise of Brahma.' In it he did something no one had done: he treated zero not as a mere placeholder, but as a number in its own right, with rules. A number plus zero is the number. A number minus itself is zero. Zero times anything is zero. He even took on division by zero — and got it wrong, an honest error that took centuries to sort out properly. Placeholders for 'nothing here' had existed before, in Babylon and among the Maya, but Brahmagupta made nothing computable: zero could now be added, subtracted, and multiplied like any citizen of arithmetic. The idea traveled west through Arabic mathematics — the Persian scholar al-Khwarizmi described the Indian numerals around 825, and his name, Latinized as 'Algoritmi,' gave us the word algorithm. It reached Europe in 1202, when Leonardo of Pisa, called Fibonacci, published Liber Abaci, demonstrating Hindu-Arabic numerals to merchants who still calculated with Roman numerals and the abacus. Europe resisted: the new numerals were suspected, even banned in Florence at the end of the thirteenth century, partly because a zero made forgery easy — you could turn a 10 into a 100 with a stroke of the pen. But place value won, because it made complex trade arithmetic practical for the first time: try multiplying MCMXCIV by XLIV sometime. Every price, every interest calculation, every spreadsheet in this course runs on a symbol that humanity had to invent twice: once as an empty space, and once — in 628 — as a number. The resistance is the point worth remembering: Florence's bankers banned the new numerals partly because zero made fraud trivially easy, and scholars distrusted a symbol for nothing. Every powerful abstraction meets this reception first. Trade math won anyway — because the merchants who adopted place value could calculate interest, divide profits, and price risk while their competitors were still pushing beads.
stories.title: The story behind zero
verifiedClaims: Brahmagupta's Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 CE) gives rules for arithmetic with zero
Al-Khwarizmi transmitted the Indian numerals circa 825
Fibonacci's Liber Abaci (1202) introduced Hindu-Arabic numerals to Europe
